visits.text: Alkmaar's cheese market (Kaasmarkt) takes place every Friday morning, from the last Friday in March to the last Friday in September, from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on the Waagplein. The cheese carriers' guild has existed since 1593: you will see carts loaded with wheels of Gouda, ritualized negotiations and the weighing at the Waag. It is the oldest and most famous cheese market in the Netherlands.
The Hollands Kaasmuseum is housed in Alkmaar's former Waag (weigh house), a 14th-century building. It traces the history of the cheese trade in the region from the Middle Ages to the present day.

Alkmaar's historic center can be explored on foot along its canals: gabled houses, pedestrian streets, and the atmosphere of a well-preserved small provincial Dutch town. Allow 45 minutes for a complete circuit.

activities.text: Rent a bike and cycle through Zuid-Kennemerland National Park: wooded dunes, semi-wild Konik horses and trails toward Bloemendaal beach. Allow for a day trip from Alkmaar.

visits.text: The red-and-white Bornrif lighthouse at Hollum has watched over the coast since 1880 and is one of the few Wadden island lighthouses you can climb. 236 steps take you to a height of 55 m, with views of Terschelling and Schiermonnikoog in good weather. Adult admission around €4.75.

The Abraham Fock Museum chronicles sea rescues organized from Ameland for generations. The distinctive local feature: rescuers used horses to launch the lifeboats—a full-scale demonstration takes place regularly in the village of Hollum. Check the calendar before arriving.

In the 't Oerd reserve, spoonbills fly over the dunes in tight formation in late afternoon. This ancient dune system in the island's east shelters harriers and mergansers. Accessible on foot or by bike from Buren; marked trails.

18th-century shipowner-captains left their houses in the villages of Hollum, Ballum, and Nes—painted gabled facades, carved lintels, gardens enclosed by brick walls. These “commandeurswoningen” are listed as heritage. An interpretive panel in front of each house traces the owner's story.

activities.text: Cycle from Nes to Hollum along the shell paths, with the sea wind in your face or at your back, depending on your luck. Standard and electric bikes are available to rent at the ferry landing in Nes. The cycle paths avoid the roads and run alongside the dunes.

If the tide is low, join a wadlopen excursion organized by Expeditie Waddenzee: walking on the Wadden Sea floor—a UNESCO area since 2009—toward sandbanks with seals is a strange experience. Excursions from Hollum or Nes, with a mandatory guide.

Each month, the Abraham Fock Museum organizes a demonstration of launching a horse-drawn lifeboat—a technique unique in the world that saved lives for decades. Check the date on the island's website before your stay.

visits.text: Amsterdam's Canal Ring (Grachtengordel) has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2010: three concentric canals dug in the 17th century, lined with 1,500 gabled houses. Stroll along the Herengracht, the most elegant, to understand why Amsterdam was the world's commercial capital during the VOC era.

The Jordaan was a working-class neighborhood in the 17th century—today it's Amsterdam's most sought-after district. Its narrow lanes, flower-draped bridges, and quintessentially Dutch brown cafés deserve an hour of aimless wandering.

The Rijksmuseum houses over 8,000 objects spanning 800 years of Dutch history, including Rembrandt's The Night Watch (3.6 m × 4.4 m) and Vermeer's The Milkmaid. The neo-Gothic building was designed by Pierre Cuypers and opened in 1885. Book your ticket online: time slots fill up fast.

Zaanse Schans is a living museum village 20 minutes north of Amsterdam, where green wooden houses and 17th- and 18th-century windmills have been gathered since 1961. Entry to the village is free—only the windmills and certain workshops charge admission. Arrive on a weekday before 10 a.m. to experience the atmosphere without the crowds.

You can visit several working windmills: De Kat produces pigments for dyes, De Zoeker has pressed oil since 1610, and Het Jonge Schaap is a sawmill. Climb onto a windmill's gallery for the best view over the Zaan River.

The Negen Straatjes (Nine Streets) form a grid of lanes perpendicular to the canals in the Jordaan. Vintage boutiques, concept stores, and independent cafés share these nine little streets: this is where Amsterdammers do their shopping.

The Van Gogh Museum holds the world's largest collection of the artist's works: over 200 paintings, 500 drawings, and 700 letters. Don't miss Sunflowers, The Bedroom, and The Potato Eaters. Booking online is essential—tickets often sell out two weeks in advance.

Vondelpark is Amsterdam's green lung: 47 hectares of lawns, ponds, and outdoor stages five minutes from the Museum Quarter. In summer, free concerts take place in the evenings. It's the perfect spot to catch your breath between museums.

Amsterdam-Noord is reached by free ferry from behind Centraal Station; take the one that serves NDSM. The former NDSM shipyard is home to bars, artists' studios and monumental street art. A side of Amsterdam that tourists in a hurry never see.

activities.text: A canal cruise departing from Centraal Station is the best way to grasp Amsterdam's 17th-century fan-shaped urban plan. From the deck, you'll see the leaning houses and the city's 1,500 bridges from an angle impossible to capture on foot. Allow 1 hour and 15 minutes.

Rent a bike and pedal through the Jordaan to the Brouwersgracht—considered Amsterdam's most photogenic canal. Early morning, before 9 a.m., it's almost deserted. Bikes can be rented everywhere near Centraal in minutes.

The workshops at Zaanse Schans offer continuous demonstrations: wooden clog making (you'll see the carving machine in action), artisanal cheese-making with tastings, and traditional baking. Plan on an hour to visit several.

The Waterlooplein flea market is open every day except Sunday, and the Albert Cuyp Market, open since 1905, is the Netherlands' largest street market. Both are less than 20 minutes' walk from the Rijksmuseum—choose one to conclude your stay.

visits.text: Built between 1684 and 1686, Paleis Het Loo was the residence of the House of Orange-Nassau until 1962 before becoming a national museum. It reopened in 2023 after major renovations, and entry is now via an underground passage beneath a glass roof that lets the light through. The Baroque gardens, designed according to the vision of William III and Mary II, have been restored to their original state. Closed Mondays; adult ticket around €21.

The Baroque gardens are impeccable: they were designed by Claude Desgots, Le Nôtre's nephew, to impress royal visitors. Symmetrical parterres, fountains and sculpted hedges recreate the 17th-century state. In spring, the flowering is particularly spectacular. Allow at least an hour just for the gardens.

activities.text: Stop by the royal stables to see the exhibition of carriages and ceremonial vehicles. The space is less visited than the palace apartments and offers a striking contrast between the splendour of 18th-century coaches and the royal family's first automobiles. Count on 30 to 40 minutes.

visits.text: The Hangende Keukens in Appingedam jut out over the Damsterdiep like open drawers. These buildings, formerly used as both houses and warehouses, lacked space when they were converted into homes, so the kitchens were extended out over the water. View them from the public space along the canal; these are private homes, not rooms open to visitors.

visits.text: The costumed actors at the Nederlands Openluchtmuseum truly inhabit their roles: brewer, blacksmith, tram driver. This 44-hectare open-air museum in Arnhem relocates authentic buildings from every region of the Netherlands and fills them with characters who talk about the past in the present tense. Allow a full day. The Museum Pass is accepted.

Arnhem deserves better than its reputation as the “city of the bridge too far”. Its Sonsbeek Park, right in the centre, hosts contemporary sculptures scattered across terraced lawns overlooking the town. The park is entirely free and little visited by foreign tourists—a real breath of fresh air.

In Sonsbeek Park, sculptures emerge from the morning mist among old beeches. The park dates from the 19th century and its landscape design makes it one of Gelderland's finest urban parks. It connects the Openluchtmuseum to Arnhem's city centre on foot in a pleasant hour's walk.

activities.text: If you visit on a weekday, the Openluchtmuseum is much less crowded than on weekends: the actors have more time for visitors and the interactive workshops are less busy. Allow at least three hours to see the brewery, windmill, farm and historic tram sections. The tram makes a circuit of the site.

At the John Frost Bridge, a plaque commemorates the battle of September 1944. Walking across takes ten minutes, and the view of the Arnhem skyline is the best in the city. The Airborne Museum at Hartenstein, in Oosterbeek, is the leading museum on Operation Market Garden if you want to learn more.

visits.text: Enjoy the award-winning beach of Bergen aan Zee, honored eight times with the Blue Flag for its exemplary cleanliness and safety. This seaside resort founded specifically as a holiday destination attracts thousands of visitors each year seeking pristine nature and fresh North Sea air.

activities.text: Try your hand at water sports on this coast renowned for its ideal conditions. Kitesurfing and sailing are practiced here in an exceptional setting, with schools offering lessons for all levels, from beginners to experienced participants.

Stroll along the long stretch of fine sand where the North Sea laps at the shore. The infinite horizon and preserved dunes create a soothing landscape, perfect for long invigorating walks to the sound of the waves.

visits.text: A ruin sheltered from the rain: the Broerekerk preserves its old walls beneath a glass roof. Devastated by fire in 1980, the church received this protective covering in 2006. The light highlights the gaps as much as the masonry; check access, since events and maintenance can affect opening hours.

activities.text: Bolsward’s Stadhuis gives you a good reason to look up during your walk through the center. The former town hall now houses De Tiid, devoted to the stories of the town and southwestern Friesland. Admire its facade, then continue on foot; save a full museum visit for a longer stay.

visits.text: The Netherlands' largest hunebed, D27, measures 22.5 m long and dates back some 5,000 years. The stones, transported from Scandinavia by glaciers, weigh up to 20 tonnes apiece. The Hunebedcentrum, right next door, tells how the first Funnelbeaker culture farmers erected them. Older than the pyramids.

In the Oertijdpark, the scent of a wood fire accompanies the reconstruction of an open-air Neolithic village. “Prehistoric men” in period costume demonstrate flint-working and cooking. Open for demonstrations only during Dutch school holidays.

activities.text: Follow the Hondsrug trails to other hunebeds scattered across the heath: 54 remain in total in Drenthe. Hondsrug Geopark panels guide you through 150,000 years of glacial landscape. The Hunebedcentrum provides hiking maps.

visits.text: An old fortress, but a largely reconstructed setting: Vesting Bourtange calls for this slight shift in perspective. The fortified village recreates its appearance in 1742, with museums that explain life within the stronghold. Start at the visitor reception to choose which open sites to visit, and devote this visit to the interiors before exploring the ramparts.

activities.text: Follow the rampart paths at Vesting Bourtange to understand its star shape from ground level. Bastions, ditches, and passageways connect around the village: each change of direction reveals another angle of the defensive layout. Wear sturdy shoes and stay on the paths, especially when the embankments are wet.

visits.text: Discover Broek in Waterland, a picturesque village of colorful wooden houses that seems frozen in time. This authentic 17th-century gem, located just a few kilometers from Amsterdam, offers total immersion in traditional Holland with its peaceful canals and bucolic atmosphere untouched by mass tourism.

activities.text: Wander along the canals lined with historic houses featuring pastel facades and admire the typically Dutch architecture of this heritage-listed village. The reflections of old houses in the calm water create a postcard-perfect setting ideal for photography enthusiasts.

visits.text: Officially a city of 170 inhabitants: the sign says “stadsgrens”—city limits—after just a few dozen metres. Bronkhorst received its city rights in 1482 and has never grown beyond its medieval core since. Red-brick houses with decorated façades line three main streets; a complete walk takes under twenty minutes. It's the kind of place you want to see before the “Instagram spot” signs appear.

Bronkhorst's chapel dates from 1344 and was once the private chapel of the castle of the lords of Bronckhorst. All that remains of the castle is the Slotheuvel, a castle mound visible on the way out of the village. The chapel now serves as a cultural centre with occasional exhibitions. It's the only standing medieval monument in Bronkhorst; its bell tower is visible from every point in the village.

activities.text: Take the little cable ferry across the IJssel to Brummen — a few minutes' crossing, a few euros. It's one of the few ferry links still operating on this stretch of river. On the other side, a short walk leads to the first IJssel levees with a view of Bronkhorst from the water.

visits.text: Explore Delft's historic center on foot, between the canals and the Markt. The Nieuwe Kerk houses the tomb of William of Orange, founder of the Dutch Republic, and its bell tower offers a view across the whole city. Next door, the Renaissance town hall dates from 1618.

Royal Delft—the Koninklijke Porceleyne Fles—was founded in 1653 and remains the only one of the original 32 Delftware factories still in operation. You'll watch artisans hand-paint blue and white patterns using cobalt oxide, whose blue color only appears after firing at 1,200°C. The visit lasts 1 hour and 30 minutes, and you can observe painters at work in the studio.

The Vermeer Centrum traces the life of the painter born in Delft in 1632. None of his 36 paintings are displayed here, but high-definition reproductions allow you to study his use of light up close. It provides the best context for understanding what you saw at the Mauritshuis the day before.

activities.text: Rent a bike and meander along Delft's canals—the city is flat, and bike paths wind around the bridges and alleyways of the medieval center. In an hour's ride, you'll pass through neighborhoods most visitors never see.

visits.text: The Mauritshuis occupies a 1644 mansion on the edge of the Hofvijver, built for Count Johan Maurits van Nassau. You'll see Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring, Rembrandt's The Anatomy Lesson of Dr. Nicolaes Tulp, and Fabritius's The Goldfinch. Allow 1 hour and 30 minutes: the museum is compact but every room is a masterpiece. Beat the crowds by arriving after 3pm or on Thursday evenings.

The Binnenhof is a parliamentary complex whose origins date back to the 13th century under Count Floris IV. The Ridderzaal, the Knights' Hall with its 18 m wooden beams, is part of this historic ensemble. The inner courtyard and the Ridderzaal are currently closed for renovation. To discover the site, walk along the edge of the Hofvijver: you can view the façades of the parliamentary complex from outside and see their reflections in the water.

Madurodam recreates the Netherlands at 1:25 scale: Kinderdijk windmills, Schiphol Airport, Rotterdam harbor, the Royal Palace. It's the perfect place to grasp the country's geography before experiencing it in real life. Allow an hour - it's fun for all ages.

Scheveningen is The Hague's seaside resort, 5 km from the city center. Its pier extends 380 meters over the North Sea, and its fine-sand beach stretches 11 km. Perfect for a late afternoon break before watching the sun descend over the water.

activities.text: A stroll along Scheveningen's seafront at sunset—the Dutch bike here from downtown along the Het Haagse Beek canal. The view of the North Sea, often accompanied by strong winds, immediately sets the tone for the Netherlands.

visits.text: A grayish military port at first glance, but the former Willemsoord naval yard hides one of the country's liveliest museums. The Marinemuseum takes you aboard the submarine Tonijn (78 m, in service until 1991), past the bunks, torpedoes, and periscopes. On clear days, they say you can spot Texel through the eyepieces. Open daily except Mondays outside school holidays.

Sailors simply call it 'De Werf'. The minelayer Abraham Crijnssen is moored outdoors - step onto the deck at no extra charge. The museum traces the history of the Royal Netherlands Navy since the 17th century. Allow an extra 1 h 30 if you visit the entire outdoor site.

activities.text: Board the submarine Tonijn: bunks stacked three levels high, ballast valves, and a 6 m² galley make you understand why crews stayed 6 weeks submerged. The Navy Games let kids test navigation simulators. Combined museum + submarine ticket recommended.

visits.text: Vast, lively and ringed by Renaissance façades, the Brink is astonishing: for a town this size, such architectural coherence is rare in the Netherlands. Museum De Waag occupies a late Gothic building at the centre of the square; archives mention its weighing function as early as the 14th century, and it became a museum in 1915. The terraces come alive from lunchtime onwards, and a market has been held here on Saturday mornings since the Middle Ages.

Deventer's Bergkwartier is one of the best-preserved historic quarters in the Netherlands, with its medieval alleys around the 12th-century Bergkerk. The Muntentoren housed Deventer's last mint until 1708; the Proosdij is one of the oldest stone houses in the Netherlands. In December, the Dickens Festival transforms this quarter into a Victorian stage set with more than 900 costumed characters.

The Dickens Festival in December: unapologetically kitsch, but the 900 costumed characters walking through the streets of the Bergkwartier end up making an impression. Outside the festival, the Grote of Lebuïnuskerk on the edge of the Grote Kerkhof offers a tower climb to 46 meters above the IJssel.

activities.text: Climb the tower of the Grote of Lebuïnuskerk from Grote Kerkhof square: at 46 metres, it overlooks the bend in the IJssel. Deventer is mentioned as early as the 9th century under the name “Daventre”. The view from the tower confirms its strategic position on the river, which explains its medieval power.

The scent of Deventer Koek has floated over the entire Brink for at least four centuries. This spiced brioche is indeed the town's speciality, sold at the Deventer Koekwinkel on the corner of the square. A bite is a must before leaving. The almond-filled version is the most popular locally.

visits.text: Their sails stand out against the sky above the quays: Zeldenrust and De Hoop define Dokkum’s skyline. These grain mills stand on the old bastions; De Hoop dates to 1849 and Zeldenrust to 1862. To photograph them together, find a viewpoint far enough back on the outer bank, and don’t count on an impromptu visit inside.

activities.text: You’ll walk along Dokkum’s ramparts to trace the outline of the fortified town. The bastions form a six-pointed perimeter, now used for walking rather than defense. Extend your walk along the sections you haven’t seen near the windmills; wear shoes suited to wet paths after a shower.

visits.text: In August, heather turns purple as far as the eye can see: Dwingelderveld National Park is Western Europe's largest wet heathland, with 3,700 hectares and over 60 pools. Two flocks of Drenthe heath sheep are led by shepherds to maintain the ecosystem. The park is officially the Netherlands' quietest zone.

Officially designated the Netherlands' quietest zone, Dwingelderveld has also become an area where wolves have returned—a presence confirmed in 2024. Visitors must keep a distance of 100 m. Watching migrating cranes from birdwatching blinds in the fall is also popular.

activities.text: Climb the observation tower near Schaapskooi Ruinen: 360° views over the heath and, on clear days, over the surrounding villages' church spires. Walking and horseback routes covering 57 km of marked trails start at the Dwingelderveld visitor center (Benderse 22, Ruinen).

visits.text: A cellar that floats to stay dry: the Edams Museum has this solution in its former merchant’s house. The masonry basin moves with fluctuations in the groundwater level rather than remaining fixed to the ground. The museum also occupies the former town hall; from November 1 to March 31, only the Coopmanshuys opens on weekends, 10 a.m.–4:30 p.m.

Colored light draws your eye in Edam’s Grote Kerk, even before the details of the furnishings. This three-aisled church preserves stained-glass windows and an old library, the librije: here Edam tells a story other than cheese. Admission is free, from April to the end of September from 1:30 p.m., until 4 p.m. in April and 5 p.m. afterward; out of season, access is only possible during events; park near the bus station, ten minutes’ walk away.

activities.text: If you enjoy short detours, Edam’s Voorhaven offers a walk among canals, bridges, and building facades. Continue to the Kaaswaag, a reminder of cheese weighing, then to the Speeltoren. The cheese market takes place on Jan Nieuwenhuizenplein on Wednesdays in July and August, from 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.

visits.text: The Van Abbemuseum is one of the Netherlands' most important modern and contemporary art museums. Its collection includes works by Picasso, Chagall, Mondrian, and El Lissitzky. The 2003 architectural extension creates a dialogue between the original 1936 brick building and a spectacular contemporary volume.

Strijp-S is the former 27-hectare Philips industrial complex, closed to the public for decades - nicknamed the 'Forbidden City.' Now converted into a creative district, it houses lofts in the Anton and Gerard factories, artist studios, galleries, and cafés in the former manufacturing workshops. This is where Dutch Design Week takes place every October.

The Philips Museum traces the history of the industrial empire founded in Eindhoven in 1891 by Gerard Philips—from the first electric light bulb to the razor, by way of radio and television. The interactive presentation is accessible to visitors of all ages.

activities.text: Wander through Strijp-S in the evening—street art covers the old industrial buildings, outdoor seating fills the interior courtyards, and local designer boutiques stay open late. It's the best place to understand how Eindhoven reinvented itself as a design capital after Philips left.

visits.text: A perfect square, and it's real: Elburg's fortified town measures 250 by 415 metres, laid out in 1392 by Duke William I of Guelders to protect his Hanseatic town. The grid plan is flawless—only one street remains curved, the Krommesteeg, because of the terrain. Parking is outside the walls, a two-minute walk away. In summer, crowds can be heavy: arrive before 10 am.

The Vischpoort is the only gate still standing since 1592, when an opening was made in the old defensive tower to let fishing boats pass. On the town side it has windows; on the sea side it has none—its windowless face once served as an oil-lit lighthouse for fishermen. Museum Elburg is housed in the former 15th-century Agnietenklooster, with free entry to the courtyard.

activities.text: The green ramparts are a surprise: the Groene Wallen Wandeling follows the 16th-century fortifications from the outside, between moats and meadows. The complete circuit is less than 2 km. Along the way, spot the Deetman ropewalk, the oldest working rope-making facility in the Netherlands, visible from the Noorderwal.

visits.text: More than 140 buildings brought together: at Enkhuizen’s Zuiderzeemuseum, you move from village to village without leaving the museum. The outdoor area brings together houses and workshops from the former Zuiderzee; the Schathuys displays boats, among other exhibits. Allow a full half day; the museum boat departs from the parking lot at Sluisweg 1.

The Drommedaris resembles a stone prow in front of Enkhuizen’s boats. This fortified gate marked the southern entrance to the town; its rounded form is easier to appreciate from the bridge and quays than from close up. For a break inside the building, head to the Drombar, Paktuinen 1.

activities.text: You’ll follow Enkhuizen’s Oude Haven to slow the pace after your visits. The basin and masts extend the town’s harbor heritage, while nearby streets let you vary the loop without returning to the car. Save this walk for late afternoon, with a jacket even if the sun is still out.

visits.text: A solar system on a living room ceiling: the Koninklijk Eise Eisinga Planetarium changes scale without leaving the house. Eisinga built this mechanism between 1774 and 1781; its planets move in real time. Added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2023, it warrants confirming your reservation before planning your morning in Franeker.

The Martenahuis stands apart from the neighboring facades with its bulk as a fortified residence. Built in 1502 for Hessel van Martena, it houses Museum Martena, devoted to Franeker and its surrounding region. First view the building from the street, then choose a few galleries rather than extending your visit at the expense of the planetarium.

activities.text: Franeker’s former university left it with a history that reaches far beyond its present size. You’ll explore the center around the Stadhuis, then the canal-lined streets: the planetarium shares this everyday setting with the town’s homes. Keep this walk short between your visits and your departure for Harlingen.

visits.text: Touristy, sure, but once the tour groups leave after 5pm, Giethoorn's canals fall silent again. The village has no roads in its historic center—only 8 km of canals and 176 wooden bridges. The Dorpsgracht is the main artery, to follow on foot or by boat.

The village was founded in the 13th century by pilgrims who dug peat, unintentionally excavating today's canals. The 18th–19th-century thatched-roof farms are built on artificial islands connected by individual bridges. Visit the Museumboerderij 't Olde Maat Uus for a reconstruction of early 20th-century rural life.

The oars of “fluisterboots” (electric whisper boats) glide silently between the gardens. Moving along the facades at water level reveals details invisible from the towpath. Go early or late in the day to avoid weekend traffic jams on the water.

activities.text: Rent a whisper boat from one of the Dorpsgracht rental shops: no license required, €15–25/hour. Two hours suffice for the complete circuit. Keep your distance from other boats in narrow passages—the canals are sometimes less than 3 m wide.

If you love quiet, arrive before 9am or stay after 6pm: the tour buses are gone and the village feels lived-in again. The northern part (Giethoorn-Noord) is always less crowded than the center, even in midsummer. Paid parking at P1 and P2 at the village entrance.

visits.text: The Groninger Museum is a postmodern building designed by Alessandro Mendini—three pavilions in deliberately clashing styles, set on an artificial island facing the station. Opened in 1994, it houses a collection of over 80,000 objects: Asian porcelain, paintings by the De Ploeg group, and bold temporary exhibitions. The central walkway also serves as a bike path.

The Martinitoren has dominated Groningen since the 15th century; locals call it “d'Olle Grieze,” the old gray one. 260 steps for views across the polders to the horizon. The adjacent Martinikerk church houses medieval frescoes discovered in the 20th century.

The Forum Groningen smells of a new library and fresh concrete—inaugurated in 2019, this glass-and-wood cube offers a library, a movie theater, the Storyworld museum, and a rooftop with 360° views. Library and rooftop entry is free. Café on the top floor.

The Prinsentuin, the prince's garden dating from the 17th century, is one of the few surviving Renaissance court gardens in the Netherlands. It offers a green retreat right in the city centre. Free admission; open during the day.

activities.text: Walk around the Vismarkt and the Grote Markt at the busiest shopping time: Groningen is a lively student city, with bustling terraces and local markets.

If it's Saturday, the market on the Grote Markt is in full swing between 8am and 5pm: flowers, Groningen cheeses, local vegetables. This is where the city reveals itself in its daily habits, far from museums. Good lunch spot: Globe, in a former cloister behind the Akerk.

Rent a bike in town and head towards the Noorderplantsoen, a 19th-century park laid out on former ramparts. From the park, the Zernike district to the north offers the chance to explore the university campus.

visits.text: Haarlem's Grote Markt is one of the Netherlands' most beautiful squares, dominated by Sint-Bavokerk - a 1370 Gothic church rising 78 meters high. The 1738 Christian Müller organ was played by a 10-year-old Mozart during his 1766 visit, and also by Handel. Admission is free.

The Frans Hals Museum occupies the Oudemannenhuis, an almshouse for elderly men founded in 1609 - and it was Frans Hals himself who painted the 1664 portraits of the regents of this establishment. The collection brings together more than twelve original paintings by the master along with works by his Haarlem contemporaries like Judith Leyster and Jacob van Ruisdael.

The Teylers Museum is the oldest museum in the Netherlands, continuously open to the public since 1784. Its founder, banker Pieter Teyler van der Hulst, bequeathed his fortune in 1778 to create a place dedicated to science and the arts. You'll see drawings by Michelangelo and Raphael, giant fossils, and 18th-century scientific instruments in their original neoclassical setting.

activities.text: Stroll through Haarlem's pedestrian streets and hofjes - these hidden courtyards surrounded by small houses, founded as early as the 14th century, are a little-known treasure. The Hofje de Bakenesserkamer (1395) is the oldest in the country. Haarlem is connected by train to Amsterdam Schiphol: it is a city of art without the crowds.

visits.text: The Hannemahuis deserves more than to serve as a place to shelter between ferries. Behind the bourgeois townhouse, the collection brings together seascapes, ship models, and silversmiths’ work; it also preserves the history of a jenever distillery. Allow 1 hour for the museum, then leave enough time to reach the terminal before the crossing to Terschelling.

activities.text: Masts stand out against the sky at Nieuwe Willemshaven in Harlingen. This harbor basin combines maritime heritage with repurposed port facilities. Walk along the public quays to look at the boats, without boarding unless invited; leave enough time to reach the terminal listed on your ticket.

If there is still some daylight after your ferry arrives, finish at Noorderhaven in Harlingen. Historic facades line this urban harbor basin, which is more compact than Nieuwe Willemshaven, where you began. Simply stroll around the quays before your final night here; you can head to the train station the next day without having to make a tight connection after the crossing.

visits.text: Fairy-tale pages hanging on brick walls: the Anton Pieck Museum set up shop in this small Hanseatic town in 1984 on purpose — its medieval streets look exactly like the scenes the artist drew. The museum, opened by Pieck himself at age 89, reconstructs his original studio in the basement with his 1,500-kg engraving press. Adult entry around €12.50.

Born in 1895 in Den Helder, Anton Pieck designed the Sprookjesbos at Efteling and illustrated dozens of books and calendars recognisable throughout the Netherlands. A drawing teacher for forty years, he stayed true to his romantic style in the face of every modernist movement. The artistic school of the time saw it as mere nostalgia; his prints still sell in their thousands today.

activities.text: If you appreciate old organs, the route between the museum and the De Fortuin windmill passes through the Dijkpoort, one of Hattem's two medieval gates. The 1742 mill is sometimes in operation at weekends. The small town can be explored entirely on foot in under an hour; the views over the IJssel from higher ground are among the most unobstructed in the region.

visits.text: Painted gables reflect their colors in the canals—here, every house tells the story of an old merchant fleet. Hindeloopen (Hylpen in Frisian) has 875 residents and once owned 100 ships flying its flag. The concentric streets and wooden bridges remain intact.

Museum Hindeloopen documents three centuries of local painting on wood, Hindeloopen's traditional costume and maritime trade. The Schaatsmuseum holds the world's largest collection of ice skates and traces the Elfstedentocht, the legendary 200 km race on Friesland's canals. A coffee or tea is offered at the end of the visit.

activities.text: Stroll across the little wooden bridges: the town is so small you can walk all around it in 30 minutes. On clear days, the promenade along the IJsselmeer lake dike offers views as far as the flat horizon over the water. Good fish restaurants around the harbor.

visits.text: Fishermen say the tide here rises faster than a man can run. The large sculpture on the dike depicting two women waiting for high tide captures the perpetual waiting that sets the rhythm of this coast. Holwerd gives access to the Netherlands' largest salt marsh area: the Noard-Fryslân Bûtendyks.

The Noard-Fryslân Bûtendyks, the Netherlands' largest salt marsh area, begins just behind the dike. The Kees Weverswadpost birdwatching blind lets you observe avocets, plovers, and ducks without disturbing them. Free access, on foot from the village.

activities.text: Take the Wagenborg ferry from Holwerd: the crossing takes 50 minutes and passes sandbanks where seals bask. The regular ferry departs hourly in high season; the fast ferry makes the crossing in 20 minutes for a surcharge. Book online for bikes.

visits.text: Roode Steen invites you to look above the outdoor tables: its facades form an open-air gallery of architecture. This central square in Hoorn brings together traces of the trading town; look for the coats of arms before heading to nearby Kerkplein. Start with this outdoor section so you don’t have to depend on museum opening hours.

The best angle on the Hoofdtoren is found from the quays, letting the boats into the frame. The tower was part of Hoorn’s former defenses; the figures of the Jongens van Bontekoe add a detail to spot near the water. Stick to the accessible areas around it and watch your step on wet pontoons.

activities.text: You’ll walk from Oostereiland to the Oosterpoort, moving from the harbor to Hoorn’s former boundaries. On the island, the buildings of a former prison have found new uses; the gate then leads to a walk near the park. Complete the loop on foot.

visits.text: Boards rather than flour: Houtzaagmolen De Rat illustrates IJlst’s specialty. This sawmill, originally built in the Zaanstreek, was dismantled and reassembled here beside the Geeuw. Check the options for visits and demonstrations; do not expect to see the machinery running without confirmation.

activities.text: You’ll walk along the Ee in IJlst, looking at the overtuinen, gardens laid out between the street and the water. These strips of land were once used to bleach laundry in the sun, a household practice that shaped the townscape. View them from the public path and respect the fences, even when a garden appears open.

visits.text: Spend a magical day at Efteling, the largest theme park in the Netherlands and the fourth-largest in Europe. This legendary attraction in the province of Brabant has enchanted young and old for decades with its fairytale worlds and thrilling rides.

Immerse yourself in the famous Fairy Tale Forest where the stories of Little Red Riding Hood, Mother Holle, and Sleeping Beauty come to life. These enchanting displays, created with remarkable attention to detail, delight visitors of all ages.

activities.text: Take on the park's six roller coasters, from classic wooden ones to ultra-modern attractions. Thrill-seekers will find plenty to enjoy among the water rides and dark rides that have made Efteling famous.

Explore the different themed kingdoms of the park that combine tradition and innovation. Efteling has preserved its nostalgic charm while offering contemporary attractions, creating a unique experience in Europe.

visits.text: Kampen's own residents call their town an “open-air museum”. It's not an exaggeration: with nearly 500 monuments in its historic centre alone, Kampen packs more heritage per square metre than many provincial capitals. The square around the golden bridge—adorned with gold wheels since the Middle Ages—and the IJssel quays form a harmonious whole that is still full of life.

Built in the 14th century, the Bovenkerk, or Sint-Nicolaaskerk, dominates the IJssel waterfront with its Gothic nave. It houses an impressive organ and stained glass worth lingering over. A few steps away, the Koornmarktspoort is the town's oldest medieval gate — you can climb it for a panorama over the river. Kampen was also the first Dutch town to produce its own cigars: the De Eenhoorn factory still offers tours.

activities.text: The IJssel waterfront stretches for several hundred metres under the setting sun. Walk the quays up to the town bridge to see the golden wheels that have adorned its pylons since the Middle Ages. The waterside terraces come alive in the evening; the Proeflokaal De Stomme van Campen, with a view over the IJssel, serves local beers.

visits.text: Admire the 19 historic windmills of Kinderdijk, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997. These 18th-century mills, built to pump water from the polders, form one of the most impressive and best-preserved groups of windmills in the Netherlands.

Visit the museum windmill to understand the ingenious workings of these hydraulic machines. These mills pump water into the “Nieuwen Waterschap,” which flows into the Lek River, allowing farmland to be maintained below sea level.

activities.text: Cycle along the paths that wind between the majestic windmills. In any season, these giants with their turning sails offer a fascinating spectacle, especially at sunset when their silhouettes stand out against the fiery sky.

Discover the history of the Dutch people's age-old struggle against water at this iconic site. These windmills bear witness to the ingenuity of a people who reclaimed land from the sea and kept it habitable for centuries.

visits.text: 32 km of dyke inaugurated in 1932: the inland Zuiderzee became the IJsselmeer, and two provinces were connected. Engineer Cornelis Lely drew up the plans in 1891 and died in 1929, three years before his work was completed. At Kornwerderzand, view the dyke and the locks between the IJsselmeer and the Wadden Sea. The Vlietermonument, with its observation tower designed by architect Dudok, is closed to the public during the works: do not plan to climb the tower.

According to Dutch historical sources, a few hundred soldiers held Kornwerderzand against a German cavalry division in May 1940, and the Blitzkrieg stopped here. Kornwerderzand remains the only defensive position where German troops were repelled during the May 1940 invasion. The 17 original casemates can be visited at the Kazemattenmuseum. Entry included in the Atlantikwall pass.

activities.text: Visit the Kazemattenmuseum Kornwerderzand: the bunkers and uniforms date from the period, and the original lock control panel is still in place. The adjacent Afsluitdijk Wadden Center opened in 2018 to put the dike's future in the context of rising water levels. Allow 1.5 hours for both sites.

visits.text: If you are looking for Pieterburen’s seals, head to the WEC in Lauwersoog now. The Zeehondencentrum moved to this center dedicated to the Wadden Sea in 2025, with an interactive exhibition about the animals and their environment. Make sure you enter Lauwersoog in your navigation app: the former Pieterburen address is no longer the location for this visit.

activities.text: Walk along the accessible quays of Lauwersoog harbor for some sea air after the WEC. Ferries leaving from here sail to Schiermonnikoog, but this loop stays on the mainland. Keep clear of maneuvering areas and bring a windbreaker: this short walk is not a boat trip.

visits.text: The Oldehove is the North's Tower of Pisa: construction began in 1529 and the ground gave way before work was finished. Architect Jacob van Aken never managed to straighten it. Today you can climb it for panoramic views over Leeuwarden and the polders. Entry €3.50.

At the Fries Museum, the scent of old wax from Hindeloopen furniture precedes the halls devoted to Grutte Pier (the 16th-century Frisian warrior), Mata Hari (born here in 1876), and the Vikings. Founded in 1881, the museum is the province's main cultural center. Open Tuesday–Sunday 11am–5pm.

Het Princessehof houses the Netherlands' largest collection of Asian ceramics, in an 18th-century palace. The contrast between the classical facade and Chinese and Japanese porcelain is striking. Allow 1 hour; quality souvenir shop.

activities.text: Climb onto the ramparts of the Blokhuispoort, a former 16th-century prison converted into a cultural center. The building itself is remarkable, and contemporary art exhibitions occupy the cells. Free entry to the building.
If you have an hour to spare, board an electric praamje to cruise along Leeuwarden's canal ring. These small, quiet boats pass beneath low bridges and along the façades of the historic centre.

visits.text: Visit Keukenhof, nicknamed the Garden of Europe and considered one of the most beautiful spring gardens in the world. With over seven million tulips, daffodils, and hyacinths in bloom, this 32-hectare park offers an absolutely spectacular explosion of colors from March to May.

Discover the fascinating history of the tulip and 17th-century “Tulipmania” through the park's exhibitions. This period when bulbs were worth more than houses reflects the Dutch passion for this flower that has become a national symbol.

activities.text: Admire the 50 sculptures by Dutch artists scattered throughout the park, making Keukenhof the largest sculpture park in the Netherlands. Contemporary art is in harmonious dialogue with the floral arrangements in a successful marriage of nature and culture.

Embark on an excursion by traditional wooden boat through the surrounding tulip fields. These old boats, once used by gardeners, offer a unique perspective on the multicolored rows stretching endlessly into the distance.

visits.text: Sint-Servaasbasiliek is considered the oldest church in the Netherlands, built over the tomb of Saint Servatius, Bishop of Tongeren who died in 384. The current Romanesque nave dates from the 11th century. In the treasury room, don't miss Saint Servatius's 1160 reliquary shrine, a masterpiece of Mosan goldwork in gilded copper and precious stones.

Boekhandel Dominicanen is a 13th-century Gothic church converted into a bookstore in 2006. A three-level steel structure was inserted into the nave for bookshelves, and a café occupies the former chancel. The international press voted it the world's most beautiful bookstore—and you'll understand why the moment you walk through the door.

The Vrijthof is Maastricht's main square, bordered by the Sint-Servaasbasiliek. The terraces stretch for more than 200 meters facing the Baroque façades: it is one of the most beautiful public spaces in the Netherlands.

Sint Pietersberg is a limestone hill south of Maastricht that's been quarried since Roman times - its tunnel network exceeds 200 km. Guided tours reveal historic inscriptions, wall paintings, and the location of a vault carved in 1944 to protect Rembrandt's Night Watch. Bring warm clothing: it's 9°C year-round.

activities.text: Stroll along the Meuse River and through the Wyck district - across the medieval Sint Servaasbrug, this historic neighborhood houses independent boutiques, galleries, and restaurants. The bridge itself is one of the oldest in the country.

visits.text: Woodwork, fabrics, and small interiors: the Marker Museum offers a close look at domestic life. Housed in six historic houses in Marken, it preserves furniture, costumes, and fishing memorabilia; the old smoke venting systems also reveal how the homes were used. Open daily from late March through September, 10 a.m.–5 p.m., and in October, 11 a.m.–4 p.m. (Sunday noon–4 p.m.); closed November–late March.

activities.text: A former island you reach by car: Marken retains this sense of contrast as soon as you arrive in the Havenbuurt harbor district. The causeway changed access to the village, but the wooden houses and narrow streets keep a pedestrian scale. Walk between Havenbuurt and Kerkbuurt without entering private gardens; save the lighthouse for a longer stay.

visits.text: To finish with a defensive silhouette, Kasteel Radboud reveals another side of Medemblik. Commissioned by Floris V, the castle kept watch over this stretch of coastline; the visit offers a look at the detention areas and views from the ramparts. Payment at the ticket office is by card only; leave time for the audio guide.

The smell of bread accompanies your visit to Bakkerijmuseum De Oude Bakkerij in Medemblik. This museum explores the baker’s trade and baking techniques: everyday work takes the place of kings and battles here. Check the demonstration schedule before visiting; what takes place depends on the day you choose.

Here, steam was used to fight water: the Nederlands Stoommachinemuseum in Medemblik occupies a former pumping station. Its equipment helped drain the surrounding area, and some of the machines still run. To see more than stationary machinery, check the operating days; allow for an additional walk from the town center.

If the door is open, Medemblik’s Bonifaciuskerk offers a break after the steam engines. This Gothic church dates back to the 15th century and recalls another side of the town around its Kerkplein. Keep this stop brief; access to the interior depends on opening hours and events, so plan on viewing the exterior by default.

activities.text: Walk to Meelmolen De Herder in Medemblik before finishing the loop along the quays. This working windmill turns grain into flour, providing a tangible extension of your visit to the bakery museum. Step back along the path to photograph the windmill with its sails.

If the wind lets you linger, Medemblik’s Oosterhaven is a natural continuation of the castle visit. Continue to the Pekelharinghaven: these basins now welcome pleasure boats in the heart of town. Stay on the public quays and choose a sheltered terrace to end the route, before your last night here.

visits.text: The Oosterscheldekering is the largest structure in the Delta Works - 9 km long between the islands of Schouwen-Duiveland and Noord-Beveland, with 62 steel gates that automatically close whenever the sea rises more than 3 meters above Amsterdam's reference level. This storm surge barrier was inaugurated in 1986 by Queen Beatrix. You can drive across it on the N57.

Neeltje Jans is the artificial island built to assemble the barrier's 65 concrete pillars. Now converted into an information center, it presents the Delta Experience - an exhibition about the catastrophic floods of 1953, which killed 1 835 people and forced the evacuation of 70 000, prompting the entire Delta Works project. The site is around 21 km from Middelburg, a 20-minute drive.

Middelburg is the capital of Zeeland and one of the VOC cities - the Dutch East India Company had its regional headquarters here in the 17th century. The 15th-century Gothic town hall borders the Markt. Don't miss the Lange Jan tower of the 12th-century abbey, visible for kilometers around.

Veere is a fortified village on the shores of Veerse Meer, frozen in its medieval setting. Its grand 15th-century houses on the quay belonged to Scottish wool merchants who held a monopoly on the wool trade with the Netherlands. Today it's a vacation destination for recreational boaters.

activities.text: Walk along the beaches and dunes of the Zeeland coast - Domburg or Westkapelle offer wild dune landscapes opening onto the North Sea. Zeeland has one of the country's windiest and most pristine coastlines.

visits.text: To understand this coastline, the Waterlandsmuseum de Speeltoren is worth more than a quick photo of its tower. In Monnickendam, its rooms link the history of the inhabitants with that of the water; images of the interior also reveal how the carillon mechanism works. Outside school holidays, come between 11 a.m. and 5 p.m.: Saturday and Sunday in winter, Tuesday through Sunday from April to October.

Set aside a few minutes to walk around Monnickendam’s Grote Kerk before heading to Marken. This Gothic church stands on the edge of town, rather than in the middle of the harbor. Its contrast with the small surrounding streets makes this detour on foot worthwhile; go inside only if the doors are open, as interior visits are seasonal.

activities.text: You’ll walk along De Haven in Monnickendam to watch the boats and facades from the quays. The town borders the Gouwzee, a body of water connected to the Markermeer: the landscape looks maritime, but you are on the shore of a lake. Keep a windbreaker within reach.

visits.text: 130 residents, voted the Netherlands' most beautiful village in 2019 by Elsevier Weekblad. Niehove is a terp—an artificial mound built over two millennia ago to protect the village from floods—and its spider-web layout has been intact since the Middle Ages. Former capital of the old Frisian district of Humsterland.

The 13th-century Romanesque-Gothic church stands atop the terp at a height of 3.7 m, once the village's only stone building. Today it houses the Wierdedorp visitor centre, open from April to October. The paths radiating from the church follow exactly the same routes as they did centuries ago.

activities.text: Walk around the terp on the two concentric paths: the red-brick houses face the center, while their barns face the fields. The view from the top across the Groningen plain on clear days is striking. Duration: a 20-minute walk.

visits.text: Marvel at the largest tulip fields in the Netherlands in the Noordoostpolder. This region northeast of Amsterdam boasts over 2,000 hectares of cultivable land where tulips create natural tableaux of brilliant colors at every turn.

Visit the Noordoostpolder tulip information center to understand the fascinating history of 'Tulipmania' and the economic importance of this emblematic flower. Interactive exhibitions reveal the secrets of bulb cultivation and trade.

activities.text: Explore the colorful fields on foot, by bike, or by car as you please. Far from the crowds of Keukenhof, this region offers a more intimate and authentic experience amid the flower fields, with views of multicolored rows stretching as far as the eye can see.

days_plan.itin_title: Netherlands Tour: Tulips, Windmills and Villages

visits.text: A reused lighthouse rather than a tower built for the island: that is the story of Vuurduin, on Vuurboetsduin. Its metal section came from the top of an old lighthouse in IJmuiden, which was dismantled and transported to Vlieland. The dune provides the rest of the height, opening up views of the island’s landscapes and the sea on both sides. Head up in clear weather to make out both sides of the island; if the tower is closed, enjoy the panorama from the permitted paths.

Tromp’s Huys brings together two seas: the one depicted in paintings and the one that sustained the islanders. In this house on Dorpsstraat, the museum brings together works by Betzy Akersloot-Berg, nautical charts, and maritime memorabilia; it also tells the story of the vanished village of West-Vlieland. Its size makes it a good sheltered stop between walks. Check the day’s opening hours, as they vary from day to day.

activities.text: You will walk from Oost-Vlieland to Noordoosthoek to view the neighboring island from the shore. In clear weather, you can make out the Brandaris on Terschelling: the lighthouse you saw the day before becomes a landmark across the water. This eastern tip lets you explore more coastal scenery without going all the way to Vliehors. Keep to open access routes, avoid wildlife resting areas, and return to the village before boarding.

visits.text: A museum lost in the forest, yet this is where the Van Goghs are — not Amsterdam. The Kröller-Müller Museum, opened in 1938 in the heart of De Hoge Veluwe National Park, houses the world's second-largest Van Gogh collection, with nearly 90 paintings and more than 180 drawings. Access requires a combined park + museum ticket; buy it online to avoid weekend queues.

Ninety Van Gogh paintings, and the silence between them. The Kröller-Müller sculpture garden covers 25 hectares of forest dotted with works by Rodin, Moore and other 20th-century artists. The walk from the car park takes twenty minutes; there are no constraints, and it's the largest sculpture garden in the Netherlands.

Jachthuis Sint Hubertus is a total work of art: this hunting lodge by architect H.P. Berlage, the former residence of the Kröller-Müllers, is one of the most important Dutch monuments. Access is only by guided tour, which must be booked online. It's located 3 km from the museum in the park, accessible on foot or by bike.

activities.text: Take a free white bicycle at the Otterlo entrance - the park provides 1,800 of them at its three entrances. This is a way to move freely around the 5,500 hectares of heathland, woodland and dunes in De Hoge Veluwe. Deer and wild boar are easy to spot in the morning on the open heathland.

If you love contemporary sculpture, the Kröller-Müller's 25-hectare garden deserves a visit in its own right, separate from the museum: the works reveal themselves around bends in the woodland paths, without signs. The Museonder, an underground museum about the park's wildlife, is well suited to children and takes less than an hour.

visits.text: The hum of insects accompanies you along the paths of Domies Toen in Pieterburen. Beside the Petruskerk, this former pastor’s garden preserves ornamental plants that have become naturalized, known as stinzenplanten. Visit in spring for their blooms and explore the narrow paths at a leisurely pace; the seals can now be visited in Lauwersoog.

visits.text: Kinderdijk's 19 windmills were built between 1738 and 1740 to drain the Alblasserwaard polders - a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997. You can enter two museum windmills and take the sightseeing boat included in the ticket. Arrive before 10 a.m. to avoid groups, or take the Waterbus from Rotterdam for an approach along the river. Plan a round trip from Rotterdam for this visit.

Piet Blom's Cube Houses (Kubuswoningen) were built in 1984 in Rotterdam: 38 cubes tilted 45° above the Blaak bridge vaults. You can visit one of them, the Kijk-Kubus, to understand how people live inside an impossible angle.

The Markthal is an arch 40 meters high and 120 meters long, inaugurated in 2014 and designed by the architecture firm MVRDV. Its interior vault is entirely covered with an 11,000 m² digital mural depicting a cornucopia—fruits, vegetables, giant insects. Stop here for lunch: around a hundred stalls occupy the ground floor.

Delfshaven is a historic district of Rotterdam that survived the bombing of May 1940. It was from here that the Pilgrim Fathers departed on July 22, 1620, aboard the Speedwell before joining the Mayflower in England. The 15th-century Pilgrim Fathers Church still stands facing the canals.

activities.text: Bike ride through Rotterdam along the Erasmus Bridge and waterfront - the city was rebuilt from scratch after the German bombings of May 1940, and you'll discover architecture unique in Europe, blending brutalism, high-tech, and urban experimentation.

visits.text: Carel Willink's surrealist canvases—camels in front of Versailles, landscapes with a nuclear power station—hanging in the 14th-century halls of Kasteel Ruurlo create a striking contrast. Museum MORE has displayed around thirty of his works in this monumental setting since 2017. Access to the castle rooms requires a museum ticket; the English landscape park and orangery are free.

Kasteel Ruurlo has housed Carel Willink's works since 2017. The initiative came from collector Hans Melchers, who wanted to offer this 20th-century realist painter a worthy showcase. The castle rooms date back to the 14th century and have been restored to combine several centuries of architecture. Together, they form one of Gelderland's most distinctive art museums.

activities.text: Locals call this maze their “dwaaltuin”—wandering garden. The Doolhof Ruurlo, right next to the castle, was laid out in 1891 on the orders of a Miss Van Heeckeren: 1,188 metres of paths within a hectare of trimmed hedges. Open from April to the end of October. It has a different owner from the museum; expect a separate entrance fee.

days_plan.itin_title: Eastern Netherlands - Hanseatic League, Veluwe and Achterhoek in 10 Days

visits.text: Kasteel Huis Bergh dates back to the 13th century — archives mention the site as early as 1227 — and ranks among the largest medieval castles in the Netherlands. Surrounded by moats, it houses a collection of early Italian period paintings, medieval manuscripts and northern European works from the 16th century. The gardens and inner courtyard are freely accessible; the guided castle tour costs €8 per adult.

The chained manuscripts in Huis Bergh's armoury and the black torches of the keep are reminders that this tower has never been captured since it was built. The castle archive, whose oldest document dates from 1227, is one of the best preserved in Gelderland. An audio guide in several languages traces the history of the lords of Van den Bergh.

activities.text: Climb Huis Bergh's defensive tower to see the lands of Montferland spread out towards Germany, just a few kilometres away. The estate comprises around 500 hectares of forests and farmland surrounding the castle. Concerts and exhibitions are held regularly in season—check the programme before coming.

visits.text: Sint-Janskathedraal is the pinnacle of Brabantine Gothic architecture in the Netherlands. Built between 1380 and 1530, it rises 73 meters high and stretches 115 meters long. Look closely at its 96 sculpted figures on the flying buttresses - dragons, angels, and fantastical creatures unique in the country. Admission is free; guided tower tours offer panoramic views.

The Jheronimus Bosch Art Center occupies a former church and presents high-definition reproductions of the complete works of Jheronimus Bosch, born here around 1450. You won't travel to Madrid to see the original Garden of Earthly Delights, but here you'll study it centimeter by centimeter through enlargements.

The Binnendieze is a network of partly underground canals that once extended 22 km beneath the streets of 's-Hertogenbosch. Board an electric boat and glide under houses, town halls, and historic cellars - a unique way to see a medieval city from below. The guided tour lasts about 50 minutes.

activities.text: Grab a bossche bol from one of the downtown bakers—this giant pastry filled with whipped cream and coated in dark chocolate has been the quintessential specialty of 's-Hertogenbosch for centuries. Don't miss the buzz of the market square in late afternoon either.

visits.text: Explore Schiermonnikoog, one of the inhabited West Frisian Islands. Declared a national park in 1989, this island offers unspoiled nature with its wild dunes, pine forests and exceptional tidal mudflats listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Discover the Wadden Sea, a unique ecosystem classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. This intertidal zone harbors remarkable biodiversity and constitutes one of the last great natural wetlands in Europe.

activities.text: Join a guided mudflat walk with expert local guides. At low tide, you'll explore this fascinating world populated by crabs, shellfish, and migratory birds—an unforgettable sensory experience.

Enjoy Europe's widest beach with its kilometer of fine sand stretching as far as the eye can see. This immense space where sky and sea blend together offers a sense of absolute freedom, far from any urbanization.

visits.text: De Kaai brings a windmill, water, and fortifications together in a single view. Standing near the Lemsterpoort, this grain mill still produces flour when conditions allow. First take in the scene from the canal; to see the work inside, check visiting days instead of relying solely on whether the sails are turning.

activities.text: Sloten’s central canal, between the Lemsterpoort and the Woudsenderpoort, remains the best starting point. The old water gates survived after the land gates disappeared, a distinction that becomes very clear as you walk. Make a short loop along the banks and fortifications, keeping the paths in front of the houses clear.

visits.text: The Waterpoort seems to set its towers directly above the water. Built in 1613, this gate connected Sneek to its harbor and formed part of the fortifications; it was preserved when the city walls disappeared. Compare the views from the nearby quays and plan primarily to explore the exterior, as access to the interior is not guaranteed.

The Fries Scheepvaart Museum is a fitting final stop for understanding the towns you have visited. Its collections connect navigation, shipbuilding, and the lives of Friesland’s merchants and boatmen; domestic interiors complement the boats. Start with the themes that intrigued you along the route, and check the opening hours before leaving Sneek.

activities.text: You’ll finish on Sneek’s Kleinzand, following the canal between the houses in the center. The maritime museum is part of this neighborhood, where water remains both a central artery of the town and part of the scenery. After the galleries, enjoy a leisurely walk; collect your luggage before heading to the station if you are leaving by train.

visits.text: A cargo of wheat thrown into the water: that is the story associated with the Vrouwtje van Stavoren. This statue recalls the legend of a wealthy widow whose pride supposedly brought about the harbor’s downfall; it is indeed a tale. Stop in front of her, then step back to see her silhouette facing the harbor basin.

activities.text: You’ll follow Stavoren’s Oude Haven toward the lights marking the harbor entrance. Colorful houses face the boats, while the IJsselmeer opens up the horizon beyond the harbor structures. End the day here with a walk; if waves reach the exposed paths, stay along the inner side of the harbor basin and by the old lock.

visits.text: Museum Klooster Ter Apel offers a quiet break after the ramparts of Bourtange. Founded in 1465, this former Crosier monastery also reveals the daily lives of its religious community through its refectory, sleeping quarters, and herb garden. Focus on these domestic spaces, then head into the nearby woods before getting back on the road.

activities.text: A short walk beats a hasty departure: the Kloosterbos in Ter Apel is a natural extension of the monastery visit. The village sits amid woods and a valley around the Ruiten Aa. Choose a walk close to the museum and return to the same parking area; water-resistant shoes will be useful.

visits.text: The salty wind greets you as soon as you reach the ferry gangway. Texel is the largest Dutch Wadden island, and Ecomare is its heart: a seal sanctuary, nature museum, and starting point for hikes into Texel Dunes National Park. Injured seals are cared for here before being released into the North Sea. Arrive for feeding times around 11am or 3pm.

Ecomare is more than an aquarium: seals, porpoises, and injured birds share open pools. Entry includes direct access to the national park dunes. Adult admission around €13, children €9. Closed Mondays off-season.

A third of Texel's surface is nature reserve, and De Slufter is its centerpiece. This polder, abandoned in the 19th century, was gradually reclaimed by the sea, creating one of Northern Europe's rarest brackish ecosystems. Visitors on foot only; dogs on leash.

Texel's lighthouse, built in 1864 in De Cocksdorp, stands 35 m tall at the island's northern tip. Plan a return trip from the town where you are staying on Texel to reach the lighthouse. Built of red brick, it overlooks the dunes and the Wadden Sea. Climb its 153 steps for views of the sandbanks and neighbouring islands. Open in season; check opening times on Ecomare's website.

activities.text: Cycle to De Slufter, the only marsh with tidal channels on the Dutch side of the North Sea. The rental shop near the Markt in Den Burg offers e-bikes. The complete island loop by bike is 54 km—allow a full day with breaks.

If you love birds, the De Muy sector shelters a spoonbill colony closely watched by local naturalists. A 2-hour guided walk from Ecomare (around €7.50) takes you into the heart of the dunes with an English- or Dutch-speaking ranger.

Rent a kayak at Oudeschild to paddle along Texel's east coast from the fishing harbor. The harbor is the island's only active fishing port; auctions happen weekday mornings. Return for lunch on-site: fresh gray shrimp cost less here than elsewhere on the island.

visits.text: From a fortified house to a Baroque residence, the Menkemaborg in Uithuizen tells the story of a changing way of life. Beyond the moats, furnished rooms evoke its 18th-century occupants; a canopy bed retains yellow silk damask from China. Book your visit to the interior online before heading to the estate.

activities.text: Move from the reception rooms to the gardens of the Menkemaborg for a change of scale without getting back in the car. The formal layout draws on the estate’s appearance around 1705; a vegetable garden, orchard, and pear-tree arbor round out the walk. Set aside this half-hour after visiting the house, and choose the appropriate ticket if you are only visiting the grounds.

visits.text: Schokland is the first Dutch site inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List (1995). This former Zuiderzee island was forcibly evacuated in 1859 because the flooding could not be contained. Since the polder was drained in 1942, it floats amid farmland like an anachronistic relic. More than 160 archaeological sites have been identified here, including 4,000-year-old human footprints.

Urk is a fishing village that was still an island in 1942 before the Noordoostpolder was drained. Its inhabitants still say they live “on Urk” rather than “in Urk.” Stroll through the winding alleyways down to the active fishing harbor, one of the Netherlands' most important.

Urk's museum traces how the draining of the Zuiderzee transformed an isolated island into a polder village connected to the mainland. Photographs, fishing objects, and reconstructions illustrate life before and after 1942.

activities.text: The walk along Urk's dike facing the IJsselmeer offers one of the Netherlands' most singular views: an endless lake horizon where the Zuiderzee sea once lay. Fishing boats return in late afternoon—the best time to see the harbor in action.

visits.text: Utrecht's Domtoren rises to 112.5 meters—it's the tallest church tower in the Netherlands. Built between 1321 and 1382, it became separated from the cathedral after the nave collapsed during a storm in 1674. Climb the 465 steps: on clear days, you can glimpse Amsterdam.

The Oudegracht is Utrecht's main canal, dug in the Middle Ages along the former Rhine riverbed. Its unique feature, found nowhere else in the world: low quays on two levels (werfkelders), medieval cellars converted into café and restaurant terraces right beside the water.

Museum Speelklok is housed in a 14th-century medieval church and contains the Netherlands' largest collection of self-playing musical instruments: music boxes, barrel organs, giant carillons, and mechanical orchestras. The instruments are played during free guided tours every hour.

activities.text: Follow the walking loop along the Oudegracht, Nieuwegracht, and Lepelenburg Park: an easy 4 km, taking about 1 hour and 30 minutes to discover Utrecht at water level, beneath bridges and alongside terraces. It's the best way to understand the two-level canal architecture.

visits.text: With 11.5 million cigar bands, the Volendams Museum turns tiny pieces of paper into monumental decorations. The Sigarenbandjeshuisje depicts the Leaning Tower of Pisa and St. Peter’s Basilica, among other landmarks; costumes and interior scenes place this curiosity in the context of local life. Locate this room at reception so you can leave enough time for it.

activities.text: You’ll follow Haven in Volendam to get a sense of the harbor before looking for a table. The boats face the waterfront shops; after the museum interiors, this walk reveals another side of the village. Opt for a short walking loop and compare menus before sitting down.

visits.text: Eight castles along 34 km: it sounds too good to be true—yet that is the reality of the cycling loop around Vorden, signposted since 1913. Most are private residences closed to the public, which makes them all the more fascinating. Kasteel Vorden, visible from the main road, is open six days a week with a freely accessible audio guide.

Kasteel Hackfort: its underground passage dating from the 14th century is one of the few parts open to the public, two afternoons a week. The historic kitchen garden, dating back to around 1790, is a must-see for garden lovers. The brasserie in the coach house cooks with vegetables from the garden. The first mention of Hackfort in the archives dates from 1392.

activities.text: Rent a bike in the village for the Achtkastelenroute, marked with yellow hexagonal signs from Vorden market square. The 34 km on paved roads pass Hackfort, Den Bramel, De Wildenborch and five other castles. A guided version is offered Wednesdays and Saturdays in summer.

visits.text: Locals call it the “toer”: the Brandaris is as much a landmark for residents as it is for sailors. Its current silhouette dates to 1594, and its role goes beyond lighting the sea: the tower also houses maritime traffic monitoring for the Wadden. View it from the square and nearby streets in West-Terschelling; there is no need to look for a ticket to climb it, as the interior is closed to the public.

In 1666, almost all of West-Terschelling burned down; at Museum ’t Behouden Huys, this disaster adds depth to the village’s quiet streets. The museum also follows Willem Barentsz’s sailors to Novaya Zemlya and recounts the wreck of the Lutine. These are stories of lives at sea, with all their risks and losses. Check opening hours before the interisland ferry; the audio guide is available in English and German, among other languages.

activities.text: You will leave the harbor to follow the Wandelroute Doodemanskisten en Seinpaalduin, along which the scenery changes while you remain in western Terschelling. The Staatsbosbeheer route connects Groene Strand, Doodemanskisten, and Seinpaalduin over 4.5 km, following red trail markers. The name “green beach” makes perfect sense here, with scenery that is much more than a strip of sand. Download the route before setting out and wear shoes suited to sandy stretches.

visits.text: Over 100,000 Jews, Sinti, and Roma were deported from Kamp Westerbork between 1942 and 1945 to Auschwitz, Sobibor, Theresienstadt, and Bergen-Belsen. Only 5,000 returned. The Herinneringscentrum Kamp Westerbork places personal stories at the center of its exhibition design: farewell letters, children's drawings, survivor testimonies. Entry €13.50.

The 102,000 stones on the former roll-call square each represent a deported victim who never returned. The twisted-rail monument, designed by survivor Ralph Prins, symbolizes transport that came to a halt. The camp site lies 3 km from the museum; the commandant's house dating from 1939, protected under a glass canopy, is the only original building.

activities.text: Walk to the camp grounds, 3 km from the museum, to see reconstructed barracks and monuments in their original locations. The audio tour (included in admission) lets you hear the voices of former prisoners. A free outdoor guided tour is offered some weekends.

visits.text: Worn objects deserve as much attention here as an official portrait: that is the strength of the Jopie Huisman Museum. This self-taught painter from Workum gives humble objects and the people around them their rightful place. Take the audio guide if its language suits you; the museum network lists English and German versions.

activities.text: You’ll head to Merk square to walk between the Waag and Workum’s Sint-Gertrudiskerk. The weigh house and the church’s detached tower provide two very different landmarks for this stop in town. Stay in the square and its surroundings: the next stop, Hindeloopen, is best visited with some time to spare in the afternoon.

visits.text: The people of Zutphen chained their books in the 16th century for an indisputable reason: theft. The Librije at the Sint Walburgiskerk, built between 1561 and 1564, is the only chained library in the Netherlands still in its original condition. The collection contains around 750 volumes, including first editions of Copernicus and Erasmus. Visits are guided only, throughout the opening day.

Sint Walburgiskerk dates from the 11th century in its oldest parts. It houses a ring-shaped candle chandelier from 1395, a copper holy-water font from 1527 and the Hendrick Bader organ of 1643, restored to its original condition in 1996. The tower can be climbed at weekends and during school holidays, for an unobstructed view over Zutphen and the IJssel. Church entry €10, tower an additional €5.

Looking down over the IJssel from the top of the Walburgiskerk tower is the reward for climbing more than 200 steps. Zutphen, a former Hanseatic city whose golden age stretched from the 13th to the 16th century, retains a compact historic centre with merchant façades fronting buildings that are still inhabited. The Hof van Heeckeren, a 17th-century town palace opposite the Walburgiskerk, houses two museums under one roof.

activities.text: If you appreciate craft beer, the Stadsbrouwerij Cambrinus on the Houtmarkt has brewed its own beers since 2006, in a room with copper brewing vats visible from the tables. The café also offers a selection of Dutch speciality beers. Count on an hour in the evening after sightseeing.

Stroll along the Berkelkade beside the River Berkel, which joins the IJssel at Zutphen: Hanseatic warehouses converted into flats and restaurants line the quay. It's the most photographed stretch in town, especially in the evening when the façades are reflected in the water.

visits.text: Built in 1409, two years after Zwolle joined the Hanseatic League, the Sassenpoort is the sole surviving city gate from the old ramparts. Its 101,000 trachyte and sandstone blocks bear witness to the commercial wealth of the era. It's open Wednesdays and Saturdays from 11 AM to 5 PM, entrance €3, and features a permanent Hanseatic hall accessed via the medieval staircase.

Touristy but well done: Zwolle's Grote Markt is ringed by 16th-century merchant façades and a café terrace tucked into the Wijndragerstoren tower. A stone's throw away, Sint-Michaelskerk displays a statue of the archangel on its roof—there's a green version in the square, look for it. Saturday's open-air market remains one of the liveliest in Overijssel.

The scent of old paper and waxed wood greets you at Van der Velde in de Broeren, a bookshop housed since 2013 in a neo-Gothic church dating from 1901. The shelves climb all the way to the vaults, and a café occupies the chancel. An hour easily slips away. Avoid Sunday mornings, when it gets crowded.

Museum de Fundatie is worth a stop on the way back: its egg-shaped roof—nicknamed “De Wolk”—is clad in 55,000 white-and-blue ceramic tiles from Makkum, added in 2012–2013 to the 19th-century neoclassical building. The collection includes Mondrians and Van Goghs, and temporary exhibitions change constantly.

Stop at Zwolle's Grote Markt square for one last coffee on a terrace before hitting the road. The square is bordered by 15th- and 16th-century merchant façades, with Sint-Michaelskerk closing off the view at the far end. Saturday's market is one of the largest in Overijssel, with several hundred stalls depending on the season.

activities.text: Take the trail around the star-shaped ramparts surrounding the historic centre: the outline of the old fortifications is still visible in the canal layout. The 2.4-km walk, signposted by the tourist office, passes beneath the Sassenpoort and alongside several towers still standing.

If the sun cooperates, climb the 236 steps of the Peperbus to the first landing at 51 metres: the tower of the Onze-Lieve-Vrouwebasiliek soars to 75 metres but public access stops there, and the view over the polders and the IJssel is already clear. Check opening hours at the basilica before coming.

If it's a Wednesday or Saturday, the Sassenpoort is open from 11 am to 5 pm for €3: a quick visit to the Hanseatic hall inside the gate is a fitting way to end the journey exploring the Hanseatic League. From the gate's opening in 1409 to today's return, the Dutch Hanseatic circuit comes full circle.
